title: GitHub - blong8334/codeLens: Visual-first progressive code review: turns a git diff into an interactive impact map
excerpt: Visual-first progressive code review: turns a git diff into an interactive impact map - blong8334/codeLens
content_html:
AI is writing more of our code. Someone still has to review it.

Coding agents can open a 40-file pull request in minutes. Reviewing it still means reading line diffs in alphabetical file order and reconstructing, in your head, what changed, what calls it, and what could break. Review has become the bottleneck, and the place where AI-written bugs slip through.

CodeLens is built to make review keep up. It turns a pull request into something you can understand quickly and then check thoroughly. It opens the PR (or a local branch) as a brief: what the change does and why, concrete risks, things to check, and where to start reading. Then you work through it in a review queue, one change at a time. Each step shows:

  • the change's own diff, with comments inline;
  • who calls it, and which callers are outside the change;
  • which routes, CLIs and jobs reach it;
  • which databases and APIs it touches.

Press a to accept and move on. The map of callers, callees and effects is one key away.

The model writes the explanations. The checks come from the code itself: the call graph, who depends on each change, broken signatures, and what each change touches. Your judgment is spent where it matters, and nothing is accepted until you accept it.

It also explores whole codebases: a written guide to an unfamiliar package, a map of its systems and modules, entry points, and hotspots.

How it works:

  • 15 languages, parsed with Tree-sitter. TypeScript and JavaScript also get type information from the TypeScript compiler.
  • Bring your own model: Claude (via your Claude Code subscription or the API), any OpenAI-compatible API, or a local model through Ollama. Without one it falls back to heuristics.
  • A content-keyed SQLite or Postgres store, so re-reviewing after a push only pays for what changed.
The brief: the author's description beside the model's take, risks, things to watch, reading order, files to check off The diff, whole file, unified or side by side, comments inline, click any line to comment
The map: callers to the left, callees and external effects to the right, grouped by function, file, module or system Explore any package: a guide written from its README and code, with a reading order

Install

Review any GitHub pull request, with no install. The brief, risks and explanations are written by the model you choose:

# With your Claude Code subscription (no API key needed)
npx @blong8334/codelens pr https://github.com/owner/repo/pull/123 -p claude-code

# With an Anthropic API key
ANTHROPIC_API_KEY=… npx @blong8334/codelens pr <url> -p claude

# With OpenAI, or any OpenAI-compatible endpoint such as a local Ollama
OPENAI_API_KEY=… npx @blong8334/codelens pr <url> -p openai -m gpt-4.1-mini
npx @blong8334/codelens pr <url> -p openai -m llama3.1 --base-url http://localhost:11434/v1

# No model: offline analysis only (call graph, contracts, risks), with plainer write-ups
npx @blong8334/codelens pr <url>

Or install the codelens command: npm install -g @blong8334/codelens, then for example codelens explore ~/code/some-repo -p claude-code --open.

Requires Node.js 22.13 or later and git. The first run with a model takes a minute or two on a large PR. After that, everything is cached by content, so later runs only analyze what changed.

Quick start (from this repository)

npm install
npm run demo        # builds examples/demo-shop, analyzes its last commit, opens the canvas

Then open http://localhost:5173.

Gesture Does
click open the card in the side panel
double-click a function re-center the map on it (breadcrumbs track the path)
double-click a group open it in place; double-click again to fold it
click +N more expand a capped column
double-click +N more files in … show everything folded into that card (overview)
− / + zoom detail out / in
← / → previous / next change in review order (entry point in explore mode)
/ search functions, files, and modules
o zoom out to the overview
1–3, Esc, Backspace switch tab, clear selection, go back

Explore a codebase

# Map any package, repository, or plain folder of code and open it in the canvas
npm run explore -- ~/code/some-repo --open

# Just one package of a monorepo (calls into the rest of the repo stay as one hop of context)
npm run explore -- ~/code/some-repo/services/billing --open

# With AI descriptions through your Claude Code subscription (cached: you pay once per function)
npm run explore -- ~/code/some-repo -p claude-code --open

# Your own model: any OpenAI-compatible API, or a local one (see Enrichment below)
npm run explore -- ~/code/some-repo -p openai -m llama3.1 --base-url http://localhost:11434/v1 --open

# A graph to share: structure and descriptions only, no source code
npm run explore -- ~/code/some-repo --no-source -o some-repo.graph.json

# Open the latest graph again (or a given one) without re-running anything
npm run codelens -- view
npm run codelens -- view some-repo.graph.json

# A specific commit or branch instead of the files on disk
npm run explore -- ~/code/some-repo --ref v2.1.0 --open

# What have I explored, and what is in the store?
npm run codelens -- history

It opens on the guide, a landing page for the package:

  • What it is: a few sentences on what the package does, and how it's organized. These come from the README and the code (with -p claude-code or -p claude, one request per explore, kept in the store), or offline from the README's opening paragraph and the part summaries.
  • Start here: a suggested reading order, each step with why to start there. Click one to open the map centered on it.
  • The parts: systems, modules, or files with their summaries.
  • Also on the page: key functions, ways in, external effects, and what changed since your last look.

Switch between Guide and Map in the header (g / m). Links with ?fn=… or ?view=map open straight on the map.

The map opens on the overview: the package's systems or modules, connected by call volume, with the databases, network, queues and filesystems they touch. Use Group by to switch between System, Module, and File; double-click a part to open it in place, or a function to center on it. Tests toggles test code. The side panel lists:

  • Start reading here: entry points (mains, routes, CLI commands, jobs, public API). ← / → steps through them.
  • Hotspots: the functions that hold the package together. They are ranked by callers, callees, how many modules they connect, and how much of the code reaches them.
  • Talks to: external effects.
  • New or changed since last look, when you have explored this scope before.

Press / to search functions, files, and modules, and o to return to the overview.

Cards caps how many cards any view draws: 25 by default, or 40, 80, or All, remembered per browser. In the overview, the least important parts fold into one "+N more files in src/lang" card per parent. Importance comes from the selection, entry points, hotspots, recent change, size, and connectivity. Folded cards keep their connections, so the map still shows where the hidden code is and what it talks to. Double-click one to show its contents, or use show all. In the focused view, the per-column cap shrinks so all columns together stay within the limit. Parts with no calls either way are packed into a grid beside the flow instead of one tall column.

The store

Everything CodeLens learns is kept in a store. It's one of two kinds:

  • A SQLite file (the default, using Node's built-in node:sqlite, no setup) at ~/.cache/codelens/store.db.
  • A Postgres database, shared by a team, so descriptions are paid for once per team rather than once per person.
--store ~/somewhere/else.db                               # another SQLite file
--store postgres://user:pass@db.internal/codelens         # Postgres, schema "codelens"
--store 'postgres://user:pass@db.internal/codelens?schema=team_payments'

CODELENS_STORE sets the default, and --no-store bypasses it. In Postgres, each store lives in its own schema, so teams (or, hosted, customers) are fully separated. Keys are content hashes, so never share one schema between parties who must not learn about each other's code. Reads and writes are batched (a few round trips per run), so a remote database is fine.

Table Keyed by Holds
parses git blob id + extractor version the extracted functions, calls, and imports of one file's content
descriptions hash of provider + function (or group) content what / why text
snapshots repo + scope, with commit id and tree hash what was explored, when, at which commit
snapshot_fns snapshot + function id each function's fingerprint, to compute "new / changed since"

Because everything is keyed by content, the store works across branches, rebases, and uncommitted edits. A file that is unchanged since any earlier run is never read or parsed again, and an unchanged function is never described again. The commit id on each snapshot is what "since your last look (abc1234)" refers to. The extractor version is a hash of the parser code itself, so upgrading CodeLens automatically re-parses with the new rules. Old JSON description caches are imported on first use.

Review pull requests

# Review the current branch the way a pull request would be (against the fork point of origin's default branch)
npm run codelens -- review

# Against a specific base, with Claude, writing the map too
npm run codelens -- review . --base origin/develop -p claude-code -o review.md -g review.graph.json
npm run codelens -- view review.graph.json

# In CI: fail when the overall risk is high
npm run codelens -- review --fail-on high

The summary is Markdown written for a PR comment:

  • the overall risk;
  • functions in the order to review them, each linked to its lines on GitHub;
  • breaking contract changes as signature diffs;
  • invariants at risk;
  • which routes, CLIs, and jobs reach the change;
  • which external systems (databases, APIs, queues) it touches.

--json or --json-out give the same facts as data for other tools.

Working through a review

A review opens on the brief. Start review → opens the review queue: one change at a time, with nothing to arrange.

  • Left: the queue, in order:

    1. the brief's suggested reading order, each with a reason;
    2. the remaining changes by risk;
    3. tests;
    4. files that changed outside any function.

    Each item shows ✓ done, ↻ changed since you accepted it, or ○ open, with progress and hide done on top.

  • Center: the current change:

    • what changed and why it matters;
    • breaking signature changes, invariants at risk, and any of the brief's risks that name this function;
    • just this function's diff (unified or side by side), with review comments inline. Click a line number to comment.

  • Right: context:

    • what the function does and why;
    • who calls it, with callers outside the change marked and test callers collapsed;
    • what it calls;
    • which entry points reach it;
    • external systems it touches.
Key Does
a accept the change and move to the next open one
n / p next / previous open change
c comment on this function (pull requests)
d the whole file's diff, full screen
z this function on the map (callers, callees, effects)
r back to the queue (from the map, at the selected change)
b / m the brief / the map
Backspace back

The map, Group by, and the invariant and diff tabs are still there for exploring, one key away. The queue is where the review itself happens.

Open a pull request in CodeLens

npm run pr -- 123                                              # a PR in the repo you're in
npm run pr -- https://github.com/expressjs/express/pull/7574   # any PR, cloned or not
npm run pr -- expressjs/express#7574 -p claude-code            # with Claude's analysis

The command:

  1. looks up the PR (title, author, description, branches);
  2. fetches its code, using your clone when you're in one, else a code-only clone kept in ~/.cache/codelens/repos/;
  3. reviews it against the same fork point GitHub's diff uses;
  4. opens the canvas with the PR in the header and side panel, including Open on GitHub and Files changed.

It also writes the Markdown review next to the graph. Fork PRs work, because GitHub publishes every PR's head on the base repository.

The PR's discussion comes along. Line comments are grouped into threads, and each thread is attached to the function it's about. That holds even for outdated comments made on an earlier push: CodeLens reads the file as it was at that commit and finds which function held the line.

What you see in the canvas:

  • Cards show 💬 counts.
  • A function's panel shows its threads (Markdown rendered, suggested changes included), with Reply and Comment on this function.
  • The PR panel shows each reviewer's current verdict, general comments, and a review box with Comment, Approve, and Request changes.

Posting goes through the local codelens view server as your gh login (or GITHUB_TOKEN). A comment lands on the function's first changed line, or on the PR conversation (linked to the function) when the function isn't part of the diff. While the page is open, the discussion refreshes from GitHub every minute, and the graph file is updated so the next open starts current.

Any website can send requests to localhost, so the server guards itself:

  • writes need a per-session token embedded only in the CodeLens page;
  • every API call must name the server as its host, which blocks DNS rebinding;
  • other origins are refused.

GitHub Enterprise: set CODELENS_GITHUB_API=https://github.example.com/api/v3 when not using gh.

Auth: it uses your gh login when you're signed in (private repos and GitHub Enterprise), else GITHUB_TOKEN; public repos need neither.

GitHub Action

# .github/workflows/codelens.yml
on: pull_request
permissions: { contents: read, pull-requests: write }
jobs:
  review:
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest
    steps:
      - uses: actions/checkout@v4
        with: { fetch-depth: 0 }
      - uses: blong8334/codeLens@main
        with:
          provider: heuristic          # or claude + anthropic-api-key, or openai + openai-api-key / openai-base-url
          # fail-on: high

On each pull request, the Action:

  • posts the review as a comment and updates the same comment on every push;
  • adds it to the run's summary page;
  • attaches the map as an artifact (codelens-map, viewed with codelens view);
  • caches the store between runs, so each function is analyzed once rather than once per PR.

Inputs: provider, model, anthropic-api-key, openai-api-key, openai-base-url, base, fail-on, comment, descriptions, include-source. Output: risk.

Any other review tool: review a patch file

For GitLab, Gerrit, Phabricator, internal tools, or a diff someone sent you: download the change as a .diff or .patch and point CodeLens at a local clone it applies to.

# In a clone checked out at the change's base revision
npx @blong8334/codelens diff ~/Downloads/change.diff -p claude-code

# Or from the clipboard, against a given base
pbpaste | npx @blong8334/codelens diff - --base origin/main --title "Retry failed uploads"

The patch is applied as a commit object only. Your working tree, index and branches are not touched. git format-patch files supply the title and description; otherwise, pass --title and --description (@file reads it from a file). Accepted changes are kept per repository and tied to each change's exact lines: download the next revision and only what the author changed reopens. (--key <id> keeps a review's marks separate.) Use --strip 0 when the patch's paths have no a/ and b/ prefixes, and --directory <dir> when it was made inside a subfolder.

Changes that span several packages (one diff per package, as code.amazon and similar tools export them): run from the folder that holds the packages, such as a workspace's src/, and pass every diff.

cd ~/workspace/MyWorkspace/src
npx @blong8334/codelens diff ~/Downloads/*.diff -p claude-code

Each diff is matched to the package whose files it changes, and the packages are combined into one review: one brief, one queue, one map, with calls between packages linked. When a diff could fit more than one package (for example, one that only adds new files), name it: PackageName=~/Downloads/x.diff. The packages are only read; the combined snapshot lives in the CodeLens cache.

Ask about the change

When a review is opened with a model (for example -p claude-code), each change in the review queue has an ✦ Ask button. It opens a chat panel where you can ask about the change: "why is this risky?", "does similar code already exist?", "what breaks for the callers?". Each question includes the change you have open, and the conversation continues as you move through the queue.

With Claude Code, it can also read the whole codebase as it is after the change: a read-only copy in the CodeLens cache, with file tools only (Read, Grep, Glob), so it can't edit files or run commands. The other providers answer from the review itself. codelens view reuses the model the review was made with; pass -p to pick another.

Your review preferences (optional)

Every reviewer cares about different things. Write yours in your own words in ~/.config/codelens/preferences.md. CodeLens uses them for the brief and for the notes on each change. Without the file, nothing changes.

Care about:
- performance
- DRY: duplicating code that already exists
- real blast radius, not compiler-checked signature updates

Skip:
- tests (coverage is checked automatically)
- renames and moves with no logic change

A Skip list that mentions tests or renames/moves takes those out of the review queue. They're listed under "Skipped by your preferences" and don't count as left to review. Use --prefs <file> for a different file, or --no-prefs to ignore it for one run.

Independent of preferences:

  • Moves and renames are matched by their body. A function moved or renamed without other edits is one "moved" item, not a deletion plus an addition.
  • Compiler-checked signature changes in typed languages aren't counted as breaking: when every caller is updated in the same change, the build checks they match.

Review your own diffs

# Uncommitted changes vs HEAD (default)
npm run codelens -- inspect ~/code/my-repo --enrich -o packages/web/public/codelens.graph.json

# A commit range, enriched by Claude through your Claude Code subscription (no API key)
npm run codelens -- inspect ~/code/my-repo -b main -H feature-branch -o graph.json
npm run codelens -- enrich graph.json --provider claude-code

# Same, through the Claude API (for CI; needs API credits)
ANTHROPIC_API_KEY=... npm run codelens -- enrich graph.json --provider claude

# View any graph file
CODELENS_GRAPH=graph.json npm run dev

You can also drop a graph JSON onto the page, or deep-link with ?fn=<node id>&lod=0..3&layer=1..3.

Systems, entry points, and sinks

CodeLens groups code automatically:

  • file
  • module: the directory
  • system: a nested package (any package.json, pyproject.toml, go.mod, or Cargo.toml), otherwise the first meaningful directory (skipping src, lib, app, …)

It also flags entry points: routes, CLI commands, jobs (including Celery and cron decorators), tests, and exported functions with no callers. It detects sinks (external effects) from unresolved calls to known clients and packages: pg, prisma, redis, fetch, axios, requests, fs, child_process, S3, queues, and similar.

Override any of it with an optional .codelens.json at the repo root:

{
  "systems":     { "Payments": ["src/services/payments.ts", "src/lib/money.ts"] },
  "modules":     { "Checkout flow": ["src/services/orders.ts", "src/services/inventory.ts"] },
  "entryPoints": ["src/api/**", "worker/reconcile.py#reconcile"],
  "sinks":       { "network": ["gateway"], "billing": ["stripe"] },
  "ignore":      ["**/generated/**"]
}

Patterns are globs (*, **, ?). path#name matches a function by qualified name.

inspect option Meaning
-b, --base <ref> Base revision (default HEAD)
-H, --head <ref> Head revision, or WORKING for the uncommitted tree (default)
-d, --depth <n> Caller hops to keep around changes (default 4)
--full Emit the whole repo graph instead of the impacted subgraph
--enrich [provider] Run enrichment inline (heuristic, claude-code, or claude)

Languages

TypeScript, TSX, JavaScript, Python, Java, Kotlin, Scala, C#, Go, Rust, C, C++, Swift, Ruby, and PHP. Run npm run codelens -- languages to see which file extensions each one claims.

For every language, CodeLens extracts:

  • functions, methods, and constructors, with qualified names (Billing.Service.run)
  • parameters, return types, async/suspend, and visibility
  • doc comments and docstrings
  • decorators, annotations, and attributes
  • calls with their receivers, imports, and throw/raise/panic sites

Each language plugin also knows its ecosystem:

  • how imports map to files (relative paths, Java packages, Go modules, Rust crate:: paths, C #include)
  • which code is visible without an import (same package or directory)
  • test-file conventions
  • route, test, and job annotations
  • which packages count as databases, HTTP clients, queues, and other sinks

Adding a language

Each language is one self-contained file in packages/cli/src/lang/, registered in lang/index.ts. A plugin is a LanguageSpec (lang/spec.ts) made of:

  1. A Tree-sitter query that tags definitions and references with a small set of captures: @fn / @fn.name, @scope / @scope.name (classes), @namespace, @call / @call.name / @call.receiver, @import / @import.source / @import.name, and @throw. The language-agnostic engine (lang/engine.ts) does the rest. Calls are attributed to their innermost named function, so calls inside anonymous callbacks still count.
  2. Optional hooks for things grammars disagree on, such as parameters, visibility, return types, or docstrings. Generic defaults cover most grammars.
  3. Ecosystem knowledge: resolveImport, selfNames, implicitThis, sameDirectoryVisible, testFile, sinks (effectful packages), and sinkCalls (effectful calls that have no telltale import, like C's fopen).

The workflow:

# see the syntax tree (node types and field names) your query needs to match
node --liftoff-only packages/cli/scripts/ast.mjs <grammar> path/to/sample.ext
# add a fixture in packages/cli/test/fixtures/<lang>/ and a CASES entry in test/languages.test.ts
npm test

The test suite fails if a registered language has no fixture case. Any grammar bundled in tree-sitter-wasms can be used, including Dart, Elixir, Lua, OCaml, Zig, Solidity, Bash, and others.

How it works

Parsing (packages/cli/src/parse.ts, src/lang/): Tree-sitter (WASM, via web-tree-sitter@0.22 + tree-sitter-wasms) runs each language plugin's query over the file. Some grammars (Swift, Kotlin, C#) exhaust V8's optimizing WebAssembly compiler, so the CLI always runs Node with --liftoff-only. It relaunches itself with the flag if needed, and parsing is no slower.

Graph (packages/cli/src/graph.ts, resolve.ts): each changed file is parsed at both revisions, and functions are matched by qualified name to classify them as added, modified, or deleted. Calls are resolved by name, without type information, in this order:

  1. the caller's own class (this / self / a Go receiver, or implicit this in Java, C#, and similar)
  2. the same file
  3. the same package
  4. imported modules, packages, or classes, including Class.staticMethod() and new Foo().bar()
  5. fields named after their class (payments.charge() → Payments.charge)
  6. a globally unique name, as a last resort. This step never applies to method names every standard library has (get, push, close, …), because map.get() is far likelier than your one get method.

TypeScript and JavaScript get type information on top. The TypeScript compiler's checker resolves each call before name matching runs:

  • a function in the repo → an exact edge (typed), even across tsconfig path aliases, new Foo() constructors, and dynamic import();
  • a library or the standard library (map.get(), fs.readFile()) → no edge, but the call still feeds effect detection;
  • unknown (any, untyped JavaScript, an interface with several implementations) → falls back to the name-based rules above.

Reviews type-check the reviewed commit, not your working tree. On CodeLens itself, the checker resolves about 93% of calls: 930 into the repo and 3,193 to libraries, out of 4,452. It takes under a second. --no-types turns it off. Calls from tests and example apps don't count against a function being public API.

Calls outside any named function belong to a per-file top level pseudo-function. Examples are CLI wiring, app.post('/x', …) route registration, test(...) blocks, and if __name__ == "__main__". In scripts, servers, and bin/ files it counts as an entry point.

Low-confidence matches are marked as such. Calls to a function deleted in the diff become dangling edges. Graphology runs a reverse BFS outward from each change to compute caller depth and the transitive caller count.

Enrichment (packages/cli/src/enrich.ts, claude.ts):

  • heuristic runs offline and is deterministic. It diffs signatures to find contract breaks (required params added or removed, type changes, sync↔async), flags protective constructs the diff removed as invariants at risk (null guards, validation calls, bounds checks, try/catch, locks), and scores blast radius from reach, exported surface, breaking changes, and dangling callers.
  • claude-code runs claude -p with a JSON schema for each changed function. It uses your signed-in Claude Code subscription, so it needs no API key. Defaults to --model opus.
  • claude sends each changed function to Claude Opus 5.5 (claude-opus-5-5), together with its callers, callees, and the heuristic findings. It uses structured outputs (Zod), server-side refusal fallback, and per-node fallback to the heuristic result on error. Pick another model with --model.
  • openai talks to any OpenAI-compatible API: OpenAI, Azure OpenAI, OpenRouter, Together, Groq, or a local server (Ollama, LM Studio, llama.cpp, vLLM). It uses strict structured outputs where supported, and tolerates models that wrap JSON in prose. It retries rate limits and server errors. Requires --model (or CODELENS_MODEL), reads OPENAI_API_KEY and OPENAI_BASE_URL, or takes --base-url: 
    OPENAI_API_KEY=sk-… npm run explore -- . -p openai -m gpt-4.1-mini
npm run explore -- . -p openai -m llama3.1 --base-url http://localhost:11434/v1   # Ollama: nothing leaves your machine

Descriptions (packages/cli/src/purpose.ts): every function gets a what / why, written in batches of 10 per request. Files, modules, and systems are then summarized bottom-up from their members; a group with one child reuses that child's summary. Results are kept in the store by content hash, so re-runs only pay for new or edited code. Pass --no-purpose to skip this step. Without an LLM, descriptions fall back to doc comments and call context.

Providers implement the small EnrichmentProvider interface, so you can add OpenAI, local models, or anything else without touching the pipeline.

Layout

packages/cli/src/lang   one plugin per language + the query engine
packages/cli/src        graph builders (graph.ts review, explore.ts explore, build.ts shared), call resolution,
                        snapshots (source.ts), the store (store.ts), enrichers, CLI (tsx, no build step)
packages/cli/test       per-language fixtures and end-to-end repo tests (npm test)
packages/web            Vite + React + @xyflow/react + dagre canvas
scripts/                demo repo generator

Known limits (MVP)

  • Call resolution is type-aware for TypeScript and JavaScript, and name-based for other languages. Dynamic dispatch, interfaces with many implementations, and same-named methods across classes can be missed there; these show as dotted "inferred" edges or are omitted. The next step is language servers for the other languages.
  • Visibility for C#, Swift, and Kotlin is approximated by directory, since namespaces and modules can span directories.
  • Renamed functions appear as one deletion plus one addition.
  • Member calls (obj.method()) only resolve to methods, or to functions reached through a namespace import, so the tool never guesses across unrelated objects. Unresolved member calls feed sink detection instead.
  • The impact map shows edges between adjacent hops only; the panel lists every caller and callee.
  • The per-change risk analysis (enrichNode) is not cached yet; parses and descriptions are.
  • A function's why is cached with its own source, so it can go stale when only its callers change.
  • Large graphs (thousands of nodes) need the planned PixiJS renderer. React Flow is comfortable up to a few hundred.

Press a to accept and move on. The map of callers, callees and effects is one key away. The model writes the explanations. TypeScript and JavaScript also get type information from the TypeScript compiler. A content-keyed SQLite or Postgres store, so re-reviewing after a push only pays for what changed. The brief: the author's description beside the model's take, risks, things to watch, reading order, files to check off The diff, whole file, unified or side by side, comments inline, click any line to comment The map: callers to the left, callees and external effects to the right, grouped by function, file, module or system Explore any package: a guide written from its README and code, with a reading order Install Review any GitHub pull request, with no install. The brief, risks and explanations are written by the model you choose: # With your Claude Code subscription (no API key needed) npx @blong8334/codelens pr https://github.com/owner/repo/pull/123 -p claude-code # With an Anthropic API key ANTHROPIC_API_KEY=… npx @blong8334/codelens pr <url> -p claude # With OpenAI, or any OpenAI-compatible endpoint such as a local Ollama OPENAI_API_KEY=… npx @blong8334/codelens pr <url> -p openai -m gpt-4.1-mini npx @blong8334/codelens pr <url> -p openai -m llama3.1 --base-url http://localhost:11434/v1 # No model: offline analysis only (call graph, contracts, risks), with plainer write-ups npx @blong8334/codelens pr <url> Or install the codelens command: npm install -g @blong8334/codelens, then for example codelens explore ~/code/some-repo -p claude-code --open. Requires Node.js 22.13 or later and git. The first run with a model takes a minute or two on a large PR. After that, everything is cached by content, so later runs only analyze what changed. Quick start (from this repository) npm install npm run demo # builds examples/demo-shop, analyzes its last commit, opens the canvas Then open http://localhost:5173. Gesture Does click open the card in the side panel double-click a function re-center the map on it (breadcrumbs track the path) double-click a group open it in place; double-click again to fold it click +N more expand a capped column double-click +N more files in … show everything folded into that card (overview) − / + zoom detail out / in ← / → previous / next change in review order (entry point in explore mode) / search functions, files, and modules o zoom out to the overview 1–3, Esc, Backspace switch tab, clear selection, go back Explore a codebase # Map any package, repository, or plain folder of code and open it in the canvas npm run explore -- ~/code/some-repo --open # Just one package of a monorepo (calls into the rest of the repo stay as one hop of context) npm run explore -- ~/code/some-repo/services/billing --open # With AI descriptions through your Claude Code subscription (cached: you pay once per function) npm run explore -- ~/code/some-repo -p claude-code --open # Your own model: any OpenAI-compatible API, or a local one (see Enrichment below) npm run explore -- ~/code/some-repo -p openai -m llama3.1 --base-url http://localhost:11434/v1 --open # A graph to share: structure and descriptions only, no source code npm run explore -- ~/code/some-repo --no-source -o some-repo.graph.json # Open the latest graph again (or a given one) without re-running anything npm run codelens -- view npm run codelens -- view some-repo.graph.json # A specific commit or branch instead of the files on disk npm run explore -- ~/code/some-repo --ref v2.1.0 --open # What have I explored, and what is in the store? npm run codelens -- history It opens on the guide, a landing page for the package: What it is: a few sentences on what the package does, and how it's organized. These come from the README and the code (with -p claude-code or -p claude, one request per explore, kept in the store), or offline from the README's opening paragraph and the part summaries. Start here: a suggested reading order, each step with why to start there. Click one to open the map centered on it. The parts: systems, modules, or files with their summaries. Also on the page: key functions, ways in, external effects, and what changed since your last look. Switch between Guide and Map in the header (g / m). Links with ?fn=… or ?view=map open straight on the map. The map opens on the overview: the package's systems or modules, connected by call volume, with the databases, network, queues and filesystems they touch. Use Group by to switch between System, Module, and File; double-click a part to open it in place, or a function to center on it. Tests toggles test code. The side panel lists: Start reading here: entry points (mains, routes, CLI commands, jobs, public API). ← / → steps through them. Hotspots: the functions that hold the package together. They are ranked by callers, callees, how many modules they connect, and how much of the code reaches them. Talks to: external effects. New or changed since last look, when you have explored this scope before. Press / to search functions, files, and modules, and o to return to the overview. Cards caps how many cards any view draws: 25 by default, or 40, 80, or All, remembered per browser. In the overview, the least important parts fold into one "+N more files in src/lang" card per parent. Importance comes from the selection, entry points, hotspots, recent change, size, and connectivity. Folded cards keep their connections, so the map still shows where the hidden code is and what it talks to. Double-click one to show its contents, or use show all. In the focused view, the per-column cap shrinks so all columns together stay within the limit. Parts with no calls either way are packed into a grid beside the flow instead of one tall column. The store Everything CodeLens learns is kept in a store. It's one of two kinds: A SQLite file (the default, using Node's built-in node:sqlite, no setup) at ~/.cache/codelens/store.db. A Postgres database, shared by a team, so descriptions are paid for once per team rather than once per person. --store ~/somewhere/else.db # another SQLite file --store postgres://user:pass@db.internal/codelens # Postgres, schema "codelens" --store 'postgres://user:pass@db.internal/codelens?schema=team_payments' CODELENS_STORE sets the default, and --no-store bypasses it. In Postgres, each store lives in its own schema, so teams (or, hosted, customers) are fully separated. Keys are content hashes, so never share one schema between parties who must not learn about each other's code. Reads and writes are batched (a few round trips per run), so a remote database is fine. Table Keyed by Holds parses git blob id + extractor version the extracted functions, calls, and imports of one file's content descriptions hash of provider + function (or group) content what / why text snapshots repo + scope, with commit id and tree hash what was explored, when, at which commit snapshot_fns snapshot + function id each function's fingerprint, to compute "new / changed since" Because everything is keyed by content, the store works across branches, rebases, and uncommitted edits. A file that is unchanged since any earlier run is never read or parsed again, and an unchanged function is never described again. The commit id on each snapshot is what "since your last look (abc1234)" refers to. The extractor version is a hash of the parser code itself, so upgrading CodeLens automatically re-parses with the new rules. Old JSON description caches are imported on first use. Review pull requests # Review the current branch the way a pull request would be (against the fork point of origin's default branch) npm run codelens -- review # Against a specific base, with Claude, writing the map too npm run codelens -- review . --base origin/develop -p claude-code -o review.md -g review.graph.json npm run codelens -- view review.graph.json # In CI: fail when the overall risk is high npm run codelens -- review --fail-on high The summary is Markdown written for a PR comment: the overall risk; functions in the order to review them, each linked to its lines on GitHub; breaking contract changes as signature diffs; invariants at risk; which routes, CLIs, and jobs reach the change; which external systems (databases, APIs, queues) it touches. --json or --json-out give the same facts as data for other tools. Working through a review A review opens on the brief. Start review → opens the review queue: one change at a time, with nothing to arrange. Left: the queue, in order: the brief's suggested reading order, each with a reason; the remaining changes by risk; tests; files that changed outside any function. Each item shows ✓ done, ↻ changed since you accepted it, or ○ open, with progress and hide done on top. Center: the current change: what changed and why it matters; breaking signature changes, invariants at risk, and any of the brief's risks that name this function; just this function's diff (unified or side by side), with review comments inline. Click a line number to comment. Right: context: what the function does and why; who calls it, with callers outside the change marked and test callers collapsed; what it calls; which entry points reach it; external systems it touches. Key Does a accept the change and move to the next open one n / p next / previous open change c comment on this function (pull requests) d the whole file's diff, full screen z this function on the map (callers, callees, effects) r back to the queue (from the map, at the selected change) b / m the brief / the map Backspace back The map, Group by, and the invariant and diff tabs are still there for exploring, one key away. The queue is where the review itself happens. Open a pull request in CodeLens npm run pr -- 123 # a PR in the repo you're in npm run pr -- https://github.com/expressjs/express/pull/7574 # any PR, cloned or not npm run pr -- expressjs/express#7574 -p claude-code # with Claude's analysis The command: looks up the PR (title, author, description, branches); fetches its code, using your clone when you're in one, else a code-only clone kept in ~/.cache/codelens/repos/; reviews it against the same fork point GitHub's diff uses; opens the canvas with the PR in the header and side panel, including Open on GitHub and Files changed. It also writes the Markdown review next to the graph. Fork PRs work, because GitHub publishes every PR's head on the base repository. The PR's discussion comes along. Line comments are grouped into threads, and each thread is attached to the function it's about. That holds even for outdated comments made on an earlier push: CodeLens reads the file as it was at that commit and finds which function held the line. What you see in the canvas: Cards show 💬 counts. A function's panel shows its threads (Markdown rendered, suggested changes included), with Reply and Comment on this function. The PR panel shows each reviewer's current verdict, general comments, and a review box with Comment, Approve, and Request changes. Posting goes through the local codelens view server as your gh login (or GITHUB_TOKEN). A comment lands on the function's first changed line, or on the PR conversation (linked to the function) when the function isn't part of the diff. While the page is open, the discussion refreshes from GitHub every minute, and the graph file is updated so the next open starts current. Any website can send requests to localhost, so the server guards itself: writes need a per-session token embedded only in the CodeLens page; every API call must name the server as its host, which blocks DNS rebinding; other origins are refused. GitHub Enterprise: set CODELENS_GITHUB_API=https://github.example.com/api/v3 when not using gh. Auth: it uses your gh login when you're signed in (private repos and GitHub Enterprise), else GITHUB_TOKEN; public repos need neither. GitHub Action # .github/workflows/codelens.yml on: pull_request permissions: { contents: read, pull-requests: write } jobs: review: runs-on: ubuntu-latest steps: - uses: actions/checkout@v4 with: { fetch-depth: 0 } - uses: blong8334/codeLens@main with: provider: heuristic # or claude + anthropic-api-key, or openai + openai-api-key / openai-base-url # fail-on: high On each pull request, the Action: posts the review as a comment and updates the same comment on every push; adds it to the run's summary page; attaches the map as an artifact (codelens-map, viewed with codelens view); caches the store between runs, so each function is analyzed once rather than once per PR. Inputs: provider, model, anthropic-api-key, openai-api-key, openai-base-url, base, fail-on, comment, descriptions, include-source. Output: risk. Any other review tool: review a patch file For GitLab, Gerrit, Phabricator, internal tools, or a diff someone sent you: download the change as a .diff or .patch and point CodeLens at a local clone it applies to. # In a clone checked out at the change's base revision npx @blong8334/codelens diff ~/Downloads/change.diff -p claude-code # Or from the clipboard, against a given base pbpaste | npx @blong8334/codelens diff - --base origin/main --title "Retry failed uploads" The patch is applied as a commit object only. Your working tree, index and branches are not touched. git format-patch files supply the title and description; otherwise, pass --title and --description (@file reads it from a file). Accepted changes are kept per repository and tied to each change's exact lines: download the next revision and only what the author changed reopens. (--key <id> keeps a review's marks separate.) Use --strip 0 when the patch's paths have no a/ and b/ prefixes, and --directory <dir> when it was made inside a subfolder. Changes that span several packages (one diff per package, as code.amazon and similar tools export them): run from the folder that holds the packages, such as a workspace's src/, and pass every diff. cd ~/workspace/MyWorkspace/src npx @blong8334/codelens diff ~/Downloads/*.diff -p claude-code Each diff is matched to the package whose files it changes, and the packages are combined into one review: one brief, one queue, one map, with calls between packages linked. When a diff could fit more than one package (for example, one that only adds new files), name it: PackageName=~/Downloads/x.diff. The packages are only read; the combined snapshot lives in the CodeLens cache. Ask about the change When a review is opened with a model (for example -p claude-code), each change in the review queue has an ✦ Ask button. It opens a chat panel where you can ask about the change: "why is this risky?", "does similar code already exist?", "what breaks for the callers?". Each question includes the change you have open, and the conversation continues as you move through the queue. With Claude Code, it can also read the whole codebase as it is after the change: a read-only copy in the CodeLens cache, with file tools only (Read, Grep, Glob), so it can't edit files or run commands. The other providers answer from the review itself. codelens view reuses the model the review was made with; pass -p to pick another. Your review preferences (optional) Every reviewer cares about different things. Write yours in your own words in ~/.config/codelens/preferences.md. CodeLens uses them for the brief and for the notes on each change. Without the file, nothing changes. Care about: - performance - DRY: duplicating code that already exists - real blast radius, not compiler-checked signature updates Skip: - tests (coverage is checked automatically) - renames and moves with no logic change A Skip list that mentions tests or renames/moves takes those out of the review queue. They're listed under "Skipped by your preferences" and don't count as left to review. Use --prefs <file> for a different file, or --no-prefs to ignore it for one run. Independent of preferences: Moves and renames are matched by their body. A function moved or renamed without other edits is one "moved" item, not a deletion plus an addition. Compiler-checked signature changes in typed languages aren't counted as breaking: when every caller is updated in the same change, the build checks they match. Review your own diffs # Uncommitted changes vs HEAD (default) npm run codelens -- inspect ~/code/my-repo --enrich -o packages/web/public/codelens.graph.json # A commit range, enriched by Claude through your Claude Code subscription (no API key) npm run codelens -- inspect ~/code/my-repo -b main -H feature-branch -o graph.json npm run codelens -- enrich graph.json --provider claude-code # Same, through the Claude API (for CI; needs API credits) ANTHROPIC_API_KEY=... npm run codelens -- enrich graph.json --provider claude # View any graph file CODELENS_GRAPH=graph.json npm run dev You can also drop a graph JSON onto the page, or deep-link with ?fn=<node id>&lod=0..3&layer=1..3. Systems, entry points, and sinks CodeLens groups code automatically: file module: the directory system: a nested package (any package.json, pyproject.toml, go.mod, or Cargo.toml), otherwise the first meaningful directory (skipping src, lib, app, …) It also flags entry points: routes, CLI commands, jobs (including Celery and cron decorators), tests, and exported functions with no callers. It detects sinks (external effects) from unresolved calls to known clients and packages: pg, prisma, redis, fetch, axios, requests, fs, child_process, S3, queues, and similar. Override any of it with an optional .codelens.json at the repo root: { "systems": { "Payments": ["src/services/payments.ts", "src/lib/money.ts"] }, "modules": { "Checkout flow": ["src/services/orders.ts", "src/services/inventory.ts"] }, "entryPoints": ["src/api/**", "worker/reconcile.py#reconcile"], "sinks": { "network": ["gateway"], "billing": ["stripe"] }, "ignore": ["**/generated/**"] } Patterns are globs (*, **, ?). path#name matches a function by qualified name. inspect option Meaning -b, --base <ref> Base revision (default HEAD) -H, --head <ref> Head revision, or WORKING for the uncommitted tree (default) -d, --depth <n> Caller hops to keep around changes (default 4) --full Emit the whole repo graph instead of the impacted subgraph --enrich [provider] Run enrichment inline (heuristic, claude-code, or claude) Languages TypeScript, TSX, JavaScript, Python, Java, Kotlin, Scala, C#, Go, Rust, C, C++, Swift, Ruby, and PHP. Run npm run codelens -- languages to see which file extensions each one claims. For every language, CodeLens extracts: functions, methods, and constructors, with qualified names (Billing.Service.run) parameters, return types, async/suspend, and visibility doc comments and docstrings decorators, annotations, and attributes calls with their receivers, imports, and throw/raise/panic sites Each language plugin also knows its ecosystem: how imports map to files (relative paths, Java packages, Go modules, Rust crate:: paths, C #include) which code is visible without an import (same package or directory) test-file conventions route, test, and job annotations which packages count as databases, HTTP clients, queues, and other sinks Adding a language Each language is one self-contained file in packages/cli/src/lang/, registered in lang/index.ts. A plugin is a LanguageSpec (lang/spec.ts) made of: A Tree-sitter query that tags definitions and references with a small set of captures: @fn / @fn.name, @scope / @scope.name (classes), @namespace, @call / @call.name / @call.receiver, @import / @import.source / @import.name, and @throw. The language-agnostic engine (lang/engine.ts) does the rest. Calls are attributed to their innermost named function, so calls inside anonymous callbacks still count. Optional hooks for things grammars disagree on, such as parameters, visibility, return types, or docstrings. Generic defaults cover most grammars. Ecosystem knowledge: resolveImport, selfNames, implicitThis, sameDirectoryVisible, testFile, sinks (effectful packages), and sinkCalls (effectful calls that have no telltale import, like C's fopen). The workflow: # see the syntax tree (node types and field names) your query needs to match node --liftoff-only packages/cli/scripts/ast.mjs <grammar> path/to/sample.ext # add a fixture in packages/cli/test/fixtures/<lang>/ and a CASES entry in test/languages.test.ts npm test The test suite fails if a registered language has no fixture case. Any grammar bundled in tree-sitter-wasms can be used, including Dart, Elixir, Lua, OCaml, Zig, Solidity, Bash, and others. How it works Parsing (packages/cli/src/parse.ts, src/lang/): Tree-sitter (WASM, via web-tree-sitter@0.22 + tree-sitter-wasms) runs each language plugin's query over the file. Some grammars (Swift, Kotlin, C#) exhaust V8's optimizing WebAssembly compiler, so the CLI always runs Node with --liftoff-only. It relaunches itself with the flag if needed, and parsing is no slower. Graph (packages/cli/src/graph.ts, resolve.ts): each changed file is parsed at both revisions, and functions are matched by qualified name to classify them as added, modified, or deleted. Calls are resolved by name, without type information, in this order: the caller's own class (this / self / a Go receiver, or implicit this in Java, C#, and similar) the same file the same package imported modules, packages, or classes, including Class.staticMethod() and new Foo().bar() fields named after their class (payments.charge() → Payments.charge) a globally unique name, as a last resort. This step never applies to method names every standard library has (get, push, close, …), because map.get() is far likelier than your one get method. TypeScript and JavaScript get type information on top. The TypeScript compiler's checker resolves each call before name matching runs: a function in the repo → an exact edge (typed), even across tsconfig path aliases, new Foo() constructors, and dynamic import(); a library or the standard library (map.get(), fs.readFile()) → no edge, but the call still feeds effect detection; unknown (any, untyped JavaScript, an interface with several implementations) → falls back to the name-based rules above. Reviews type-check the reviewed commit, not your working tree. On CodeLens itself, the checker resolves about 93% of calls: 930 into the repo and 3,193 to libraries, out of 4,452. It takes under a second. --no-types turns it off. Calls from tests and example apps don't count against a function being public API. Calls outside any named function belong to a per-file top level pseudo-function. Examples are CLI wiring, app.post('/x', …) route registration, test(...) blocks, and if __name__ == "__main__". In scripts, servers, and bin/ files it counts as an entry point. Low-confidence matches are marked as such. Calls to a function deleted in the diff become dangling edges. Graphology runs a reverse BFS outward from each change to compute caller depth and the transitive caller count. Enrichment (packages/cli/src/enrich.ts, claude.ts): heuristic runs offline and is deterministic. It diffs signatures to find contract breaks (required params added or removed, type changes, sync↔async), flags protective constructs the diff removed as invariants at risk (null guards, validation calls, bounds checks, try/catch, locks), and scores blast radius from reach, exported surface, breaking changes, and dangling callers. claude-code runs claude -p with a JSON schema for each changed function. It uses your signed-in Claude Code subscription, so it needs no API key. Defaults to --model opus. claude sends each changed function to Claude Opus 5.5 (claude-opus-5-5), together with its callers, callees, and the heuristic findings. It uses structured outputs (Zod), server-side refusal fallback, and per-node fallback to the heuristic result on error. Pick another model with --model. openai talks to any OpenAI-compatible API: OpenAI, Azure OpenAI, OpenRouter, Together, Groq, or a local server (Ollama, LM Studio, llama.cpp, vLLM). It uses strict structured outputs where supported, and tolerates models that wrap JSON in prose. It retries rate limits and server errors. Requires --model (or CODELENS_MODEL), reads OPENAI_API_KEY and OPENAI_BASE_URL, or takes --base-url: OPENAI_API_KEY=sk-… npm run explore -- . -p openai -m gpt-4.1-mini npm run explore -- . -p openai -m llama3.1 --base-url http://localhost:11434/v1 # Ollama: nothing leaves your machine Descriptions (packages/cli/src/purpose.ts): every function gets a what / why, written in batches of 10 per request. Files, modules, and systems are then summarized bottom-up from their members; a group with one child reuses that child's summary. Results are kept in the store by content hash, so re-runs only pay for new or edited code. Pass --no-purpose to skip this step. Without an LLM, descriptions fall back to doc comments and call context. Providers implement the small EnrichmentProvider interface, so you can add OpenAI, local models, or anything else without touching the pipeline. Layout packages/cli/src/lang one plugin per language + the query engine packages/cli/src graph builders (graph.ts review, explore.ts explore, build.ts shared), call resolution, snapshots (source.ts), the store (store.ts), enrichers, CLI (tsx, no build step) packages/cli/test per-language fixtures and end-to-end repo tests (npm test) packages/web Vite + React + @xyflow/react + dagre canvas scripts/ demo repo generator Known limits (MVP) Call resolution is type-aware for TypeScript and JavaScript, and name-based for other languages. Dynamic dispatch, interfaces with many implementations, and same-named methods across classes can be missed there; these show as dotted "inferred" edges or are omitted. The next step is language servers for the other languages. Visibility for C#, Swift, and Kotlin is approximated by directory, since namespaces and modules can span directories. Renamed functions appear as one deletion plus one addition. Member calls (obj.method()) only resolve to methods, or to functions reached through a namespace import, so the tool never guesses across unrelated objects. Unresolved member calls feed sink detection instead. The impact map shows edges between adjacent hops only; the panel lists every caller and callee. The per-change risk analysis (enrichNode) is not cached yet; parses and descriptions are. A function's why is cached with its own source, so it can go stale when only its callers change. Large graphs (thousands of nodes) need the planned PixiJS renderer. React Flow is comfortable up to a few hundred. License Apache-2.0. See LICENSE and NOTICE. Releasing npm run pack # builds packages/cli (bundle + canvas) and writes the .tgz npm would publish npm publish -w @blong8334/codelens prepack builds the CLI bundle and the canvas into packages/cli/dist, and copies README, LICENSE and NOTICE in. Local graph files are never included.

content_html_zh:
AI is writing more of our code. Someone still has to review it.

Coding agents can open a 40-file pull request in minutes. Reviewing it still means reading line diffs in alphabetical file order and reconstructing, in your head, what changed, what calls it, and what could break. Review has become the bottleneck, and the place where AI-written bugs slip through.

CodeLens is built to make review keep up. It turns a pull request into something you can understand quickly and then check thoroughly. It opens the PR (or a local branch) as a brief: what the change does and why, concrete risks, things to check, and where to start reading. Then you work through it in a review queue, one change at a time. Each step shows:

  • the change's own diff, with comments inline;
  • who calls it, and which callers are outside the change;
  • which routes, CLIs and jobs reach it;
  • which databases and APIs it touches.

Press a to accept and move on. The map of callers, callees and effects is one key away.

The model writes the explanations. The checks come from the code itself: the call graph, who depends on each change, broken signatures, and what each change touches. Your judgment is spent where it matters, and nothing is accepted until you accept it.

It also explores whole codebases: a written guide to an unfamiliar package, a map of its systems and modules, entry points, and hotspots.

工作原理：

  • 15 languages, parsed with Tree-sitter. TypeScript and JavaScript also get type information from the TypeScript compiler.
  • Bring your own model: Claude (via your Claude Code subscription or the API), any OpenAI-compatible API, or a local model through Ollama. Without one it falls back to heuristics.
  • A content-keyed SQLite or Postgres store, so re-reviewing after a push only pays for what changed.
The brief: the author's description beside the model's take, risks, things to watch, reading order, files to check off The diff, whole file, unified or side by side, comments inline, click any line to comment
The map: callers to the left, callees and external effects to the right, grouped by function, file, module or system Explore any package: a guide written from its README and code, with a reading order

安装

Review any GitHub pull request, with no install. The brief, risks and explanations are written by the model you choose:

# With your Claude Code subscription (no API key needed)
npx @blong8334/codelens pr https://github.com/owner/repo/pull/123 -p claude-code

# With an Anthropic API key
ANTHROPIC_API_KEY=… npx @blong8334/codelens pr <url> -p claude

# With OpenAI, or any OpenAI-compatible endpoint such as a local Ollama
OPENAI_API_KEY=… npx @blong8334/codelens pr <url> -p openai -m gpt-4.1-mini
npx @blong8334/codelens pr <url> -p openai -m llama3.1 --base-url http://localhost:11434/v1

# No model: offline analysis only (call graph, contracts, risks), with plainer write-ups
npx @blong8334/codelens pr <url>

Or install the codelens command: npm install -g @blong8334/codelens, then for example codelens explore ~/code/some-repo -p claude-code --open.

Requires Node.js 22.13 or later and git. The first run with a model takes a minute or two on a large PR. After that, everything is cached by content, so later runs only analyze what changed.

Quick start (from this repository)

npm install
npm run demo        # builds examples/demo-shop, analyzes its last commit, opens the canvas

Then open http://localhost:5173.

手势 Does
click open the card in the side panel
double-click a function re-center the map on it (breadcrumbs track the path)
double-click a group open it in place; double-click again to fold it
click +N more expand a capped column
double-click +N more files in … show everything folded into that card (overview)
− / + zoom detail out / in
← / → previous / next change in review order (entry point in explore mode)
/ search functions, files, and modules
o zoom out to the overview
1–3, Esc, Backspace switch tab, clear selection, go back

Explore a codebase

# Map any package, repository, or plain folder of code and open it in the canvas
npm run explore -- ~/code/some-repo --open

# Just one package of a monorepo (calls into the rest of the repo stay as one hop of context)
npm run explore -- ~/code/some-repo/services/billing --open

# With AI descriptions through your Claude Code subscription (cached: you pay once per function)
npm run explore -- ~/code/some-repo -p claude-code --open

# Your own model: any OpenAI-compatible API, or a local one (see Enrichment below)
npm run explore -- ~/code/some-repo -p openai -m llama3.1 --base-url http://localhost:11434/v1 --open

# A graph to share: structure and descriptions only, no source code
npm run explore -- ~/code/some-repo --no-source -o some-repo.graph.json

# Open the latest graph again (or a given one) without re-running anything
npm run codelens -- view
npm run codelens -- view some-repo.graph.json

# A specific commit or branch instead of the files on disk
npm run explore -- ~/code/some-repo --ref v2.1.0 --open

# What have I explored, and what is in the store?
npm run codelens -- history

It opens on the guide, a landing page for the package:

  • What it is: a few sentences on what the package does, and how it's organized. These come from the README and the code (with -p claude-code or -p claude, one request per explore, kept in the store), or offline from the README's opening paragraph and the part summaries.
  • Start here: a suggested reading order, each step with why to start there. Click one to open the map centered on it.
  • The parts: systems, modules, or files with their summaries.
  • Also on the page: key functions, ways in, external effects, and what changed since your last look.

Switch between Guide and Map in the header (g / m). Links with ?fn=… or ?view=map open straight on the map.

The map opens on the overview: the package's systems or modules, connected by call volume, with the databases, network, queues and filesystems they touch. Use Group by to switch between System, Module, and File; double-click a part to open it in place, or a function to center on it. Tests toggles test code. The side panel lists:

  • Start reading here: entry points (mains, routes, CLI commands, jobs, public API). ← / → steps through them.
  • Hotspots: the functions that hold the package together. They are ranked by callers, callees, how many modules they connect, and how much of the code reaches them.
  • Talks to: external effects.
  • New or changed since last look, when you have explored this scope before.

Press / to search functions, files, and modules, and o to return to the overview.

Cards caps how many cards any view draws: 25 by default, or 40, 80, or All, remembered per browser. In the overview, the least important parts fold into one "+N more files in src/lang" card per parent. Importance comes from the selection, entry points, hotspots, recent change, size, and connectivity. Folded cards keep their connections, so the map still shows where the hidden code is and what it talks to. Double-click one to show its contents, or use show all. In the focused view, the per-column cap shrinks so all columns together stay within the limit. Parts with no calls either way are packed into a grid beside the flow instead of one tall column.

The store

Everything CodeLens learns is kept in a store. It's one of two kinds:

  • A SQLite file (the default, using Node's built-in node:sqlite, no setup) at ~/.cache/codelens/store.db.
  • A Postgres database, shared by a team, so descriptions are paid for once per team rather than once per person.
--store ~/somewhere/else.db                               # another SQLite file
--store postgres://user:pass@db.internal/codelens         # Postgres, schema "codelens"
--store 'postgres://user:pass@db.internal/codelens?schema=team_payments'

CODELENS_STORE sets the default, and --no-store bypasses it. In Postgres, each store lives in its own schema, so teams (or, hosted, customers) are fully separated. Keys are content hashes, so never share one schema between parties who must not learn about each other's code. Reads and writes are batched (a few round trips per run), so a remote database is fine.

Table Keyed by Holds
parses git blob id + extractor version the extracted functions, calls, and imports of one file's content
descriptions hash of provider + function (or group) content what / why text
snapshots repo + scope, with commit id and tree hash what was explored, when, at which commit
snapshot_fns snapshot + function id each function's fingerprint, to compute "new / changed since"

Because everything is keyed by content, the store works across branches, rebases, and uncommitted edits. A file that is unchanged since any earlier run is never read or parsed again, and an unchanged function is never described again. The commit id on each snapshot is what "since your last look (abc1234)" refers to. The extractor version is a hash of the parser code itself, so upgrading CodeLens automatically re-parses with the new rules. Old JSON description caches are imported on first use.

Review pull requests

# Review the current branch the way a pull request would be (against the fork point of origin's default branch)
npm run codelens -- review

# Against a specific base, with Claude, writing the map too
npm run codelens -- review . --base origin/develop -p claude-code -o review.md -g review.graph.json
npm run codelens -- view review.graph.json

# In CI: fail when the overall risk is high
npm run codelens -- review --fail-on high

The summary is Markdown written for a PR comment:

  • the overall risk;
  • functions in the order to review them, each linked to its lines on GitHub;
  • breaking contract changes as signature diffs;
  • invariants at risk;
  • which routes, CLIs, and jobs reach the change;
  • which external systems (databases, APIs, queues) it touches.

--json or --json-out give the same facts as data for other tools.

Working through a review

A review opens on the brief. Start review → opens the review queue: one change at a time, with nothing to arrange.

  • Left: the queue, in order: the brief's suggested reading order, each with a reason; the remaining changes by risk; tests; files that changed outside any function. Each item shows ✓ done, ↻ changed since you accepted it, or ○ open, with progress and hide done on top.
  • Center: the current change: what changed and why it matters; breaking signature changes, invariants at risk, and any of the brief's risks that name this function; just this function's diff (unified or side by side), with review comments inline. Click a line number to comment.
  • Right: context: what the function does and why; who calls it, with callers outside the change marked and test callers collapsed; what it calls; which entry points reach it; external systems it touches.

Open a pull request in CodeLens

npm run pr -- 123                                              # a PR in the repo you're in
npm run pr -- https://github.com/expressjs/express/pull/7574   # any PR, cloned or not
npm run pr -- expressjs/express#7574 -p claude-code            # with Claude's analysis

The command:

  1. looks up the PR (title, author, description, branches);
  2. fetches its code, using your clone when you're in one, else a code-only clone kept in ~/.cache/codelens/repos/;
  3. reviews it against the same fork point GitHub's diff uses;
  4. opens the canvas with the PR in the header and side panel, including Open on GitHub and Files changed.

It also writes the Markdown review next to the graph. Fork PRs work, because GitHub publishes every PR's head on the base repository.

The PR's discussion comes along. Line comments are grouped into threads, and each thread is attached to the function it's about. That holds even for outdated comments made on an earlier push: CodeLens reads the file as it was at that commit and finds which function held the line.

What you see in the canvas:

  • Cards show 💬 counts.
  • A function's panel shows its threads (Markdown rendered, suggested changes included), with Reply and Comment on this function.
  • The PR panel shows each reviewer's current verdict, general comments, and a review box with Comment, Approve, and Request changes.

Posting goes through the local codelens view server as your gh login (or GITHUB_TOKEN). A comment lands on the function's first changed line, or on the PR conversation (linked to the function) when the function isn't part of the diff. While the page is open, the discussion refreshes from GitHub every minute, and the graph file is updated so the next open starts current.

Any website can send requests to localhost, so the server guards itself:

  • writes need a per-session token embedded only in the CodeLens page;
  • every API call must name the server as its host, which blocks DNS rebinding;
  • other origins are refused.

GitHub Enterprise: set CODELENS_GITHUB_API=https://github.example.com/api/v3 when not using gh.

Auth: it uses your gh login when you're signed in (private repos and GitHub Enterprise), else GITHUB_TOKEN; public repos need neither.

Any other review tool: review a patch file

For GitLab, Gerrit, Phabricator, internal tools, or a diff someone sent you: download the change as a .diff or .patch and point CodeLens at a local clone it applies to.

# In a clone checked out at the change's base revision
npx @blong8334/codelens diff ~/Downloads/change.diff -p claude-code

# Or from the clipboard, against a given base
pbpaste | npx @blong8334/codelens diff - --base origin/main --title "Retry failed uploads"

The patch is applied as a commit object only. Your working tree, index and branches are not touched. git format-patch files supply the title and description; otherwise, pass --title and --description (@file reads it from a file). Accepted changes are kept per repository and tied to each change's exact lines: download the next revision and only what the author changed reopens. (--key <id> keeps a review's marks separate.) Use --strip 0 when the patch's paths have no a/ and b/ prefixes, and --directory <dir> when it was made inside a subfolder.

Changes that span several packages (one diff per package, as code.amazon and similar tools export them): run from the folder that holds the packages, such as a workspace's src/, and pass every diff.

cd ~/workspace/MyWorkspace/src
npx @blong8334/codelens diff ~/Downloads/*.diff -p claude-code

Each diff is matched to the package whose files it changes, and the packages are combined into one review: one brief, one queue, one map, with calls between packages linked. When a diff could fit more than one package (for example, one that only adds new files), name it: PackageName=~/Downloads/x.diff. The packages are only read; the combined snapshot lives in the CodeLens cache.

Ask about the change

When a review is opened with a model (for example -p claude-code), each change in the review queue has an ✦ Ask button. It opens a chat panel where you can ask about the change: "why is this risky?", "does similar code already exist?", "what breaks for the callers?". Each question includes the change you have open, and the conversation continues as you move through the queue.

With Claude Code, it can also read the whole codebase as it is after the change: a read-only copy in the CodeLens cache, with file tools only (Read, Grep, Glob), so it can't edit files or run commands. The other providers answer from the review itself. codelens view reuses the model the review was made with; pass -p to pick another.

Your review preferences (optional)

Every reviewer cares about different things. Write yours in your own words in ~/.config/codelens/preferences.md. CodeLens uses them for the brief and for the notes on each change. Without the file, nothing changes.

Care about:
- performance
- DRY: duplicating code that already exists
- real blast radius, not compiler-checked signature updates

Skip:
- tests (coverage is checked automatically)
- renames and moves with no logic change

A Skip list that mentions tests or renames/moves takes those out of the review queue. They're listed under "Skipped by your preferences" and don't count as left to review. Use --prefs <file> for a different file, or --no-prefs to ignore it for one run.

Independent of preferences:

  • Moves and renames are matched by their body. A function moved or renamed without other edits is one "moved" item, not a deletion plus an addition.
  • Compiler-checked signature changes in typed languages aren't counted as breaking: when every caller is updated in the same change, the build checks they match.

Systems, entry points, and sinks

CodeLens groups code automatically:

  • file
  • module: the directory
  • system: a nested package (any package.json, pyproject.toml, go.mod, or Cargo.toml), otherwise the first meaningful directory (skipping src, lib, app, …)

It also flags entry points: routes, CLI commands, jobs (including Celery and cron decorators), tests, and exported functions with no callers. It detects sinks (external effects) from unresolved calls to known clients and packages: pg, prisma, redis, fetch, axios, requests, fs, child_process, S3, queues, and similar.

Override any of it with an optional .codelens.json at the repo root:

{
  "systems":     { "Payments": ["src/services/payments.ts", "src/lib/money.ts"] },
  "modules":     { "Checkout flow": ["src/services/orders.ts", "src/services/inventory.ts"] },
  "entryPoints": ["src/api/**", "worker/reconcile.py#reconcile"],
  "sinks":       { "network": ["gateway"], "billing": ["stripe"] },
  "ignore":      ["**/generated/**"]
}

Patterns are globs (*, **, ?). path#name matches a function by qualified name.

-d, --depth <n> Caller hops to keep around changes (default 4)
